newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour to cut taxes - report.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour to cut taxes - report.

text.p: The opposition Labour Party, long branded Britain's tax-and-spend party, will unveil plans next month to cut middle-class taxes in an all-out drive to win the next election, the Sunday Times said.

The paper said Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown believed his proposed tax cut would be popular with a crucial group of voters who were suspicious of Labour's tax and spending plans at the last election.
The plan would cut taxes for hundreds of thousands of voters who earn 30,000 pounds ($50,390) to 35,000 pounds ($58,790) a year and currently pay the top tax rate of 40 percent.

Brown will argue that his proposal is in line with Labour's promise of "fair taxation" and would be self-financing, said the Sunday Times. To pay for tax cuts, it said Brown would abolish some tax reliefs and allowances.

Labour's tax plans have been eagerly awaited by the ruling Conservatives as they strive to hold on to power. With Labour some 20 points ahead in the polls and an election due by May 22, taxes are considered a key issue by both parties.
Labour leader Tony Blair has said the cumulative effect of tax rises since 1992 were equivalent to seven percentage points on income tax.
The Conservatives have traditionally donned the tax-cutting mantle but the economic policy gap between the major parties has narrowed considerably in recent years.

Last week, finance minister Kenneth Clarke delivered a cautious budget that ignored calls by right-wingers for big tax cuts. Clarke sliced just one penny off income tax -- a move he billed as prudent but which few believed would win votes.
Conservatives held power at the last election in large part by playing to voters' fears that Labour would raise taxes and pump money into costly state projects.
